;1;0;372.6;422.1;235.8;235.8!S;20;36;1;245,10,10;20.7;150.3;258.3;258.3!S;36;48;1;246,9,9;150.3;324;258.3;258.3!S;48;21;1;0;324;423;258.3;258.3!S;22;36;1;247,8,8;20.7;150.3;279.90000000000003;279.90000000000003!S;36;49;1;243,18,18;150.3;372.6;279.90000000000003;279.90000000000003!S;49;23;1;0;372.6;423;279.90000000000003;279.90000000000003!S;24;36;1;244,16,16;22.5;150.3;300.6;300.6!S;36;50;1;246,14,14;150.3;324.90000000000003;300.6;300.6!S;50;25;1;0;324.90000000000003;425.7;300.6;300.6!S;26;36;1;245,20,20;21.6;150.3;322.2;322.2!S;36;51;1;248,13,13;150.3;372.6;322.2;322.2!S;51;27;1;0;372.6;425.7;322.2;322.2!S;28;36;1;240,15,15;24.3;150.3;342.90000000000003;342.90000000000003!S;36;52;1;242,13,13;150.3;326.7;342.90000000000003;342.90000000000003!S;52;29;1;0;326.7;426.6;342.90000000000003;342.90000000000003!S;30;36;1;243,18,18;19.8;150.3;366.3;366.3!S;36;53;1;237,12,12;150.3;373.5;366.3;366.3!S;53;31;1;0;373.5;425.7;366.3;366.3!S;32;36;1;239,11,11;19.8;150.3;388.8;388.8!S;36;54;1;243,18,18;150.3;328.5;388.8;388.8!S;54;33;1;0;328.5;426.6;388.8;388.8!S;34;36;1;234,11,11;20.7;150.3;407.7;407.7!S;36;55;1;251,24,24;150.3;376.2;407.7;407.7!S;55;35;1;0;376.2;426.6;407.7;407.7!T;GOAL: We want to find the prime factors of N = 21, so 3 and 7.
Shor's algorithm is probabilistic, meaning we do not necessarily find these factors on the first measurement.

The algorithm must find the order r which,  for an integer a < 21, is the smallest k such that: a**k≡ 1 (mod 21)

The number of qBits needed for each register must be n such that 2**n>=N**2  
Here, 9 qbits since 2**9 = 512  is greater than 21**2 = 441

First possibility: "Winning the lottery". We randomly find a divisor of N, and the algorithm stops.

Otherwise:
In this simulation, a and r must satisfy the 2 hypotheses below:

- hyp 1 : r is even
- hyp 2 : a **(r/2) + 1 must not be divisible by 21

For this simulation, if one of these 2 hypotheses is not verified, we choose another value of a and restart.

A third hypothesis is tested but will not be verified here:

- hyp 3 : The order r must divide 2**n   where n is the number of qbits, here 9

Practical Steps:
- We must change the oracle function with the chosen value of a (e.g., for a = 2, write return (2**X) % 21,)
- We perform a partial measurement of the second register (the last 9 bits)
- For the first register, we look at the possible measurements m in the "Probas" window

Since hypothesis 3 is not verified, we obtain many possible states.
We retain only those with the highest probabilities, here for the 1st register:
0, 85, 171, 256, 341, 427

We compute for these different possible measurements m: the value m/(2**n), 2 situations:
  1- If we obtain an integer → failure... we restart
2- If we obtain a fraction, we must find an approximation with a denominator smaller than 21 using the continued fractions method
Example: If we measure 427, the Euclidean algorithm gives the factors:
427 = 0 × 512 + 1 × 427
427 = 1 × 427 + 85
427 = 5 × 85 + 2
Thus,
427 / 512 = (0 + 1 / (1 + 1 / 5)) = 5 / 6

Since 6 is much smaller than 21, we verify that:
2**6≡ 1 (mod 21)
Thus, the order r = 6

If this was not the case, we would repeat a measurement.

Finding the Factors
Once r = 6 is determined, we obtain two factors d1 and d2 of N such that:
d1 = PGCD(a**r/2 +1) and d2 = PGCD(a**r/2 -1)
 Thus, here: 3 and 7

Testing Different Values of a
In this simulation, you can choose other values of a to test while verifying that hypotheses 1 and 2 are satisfied.
